title: Multilayer Recurrent Network Models of Primate Retinal Ganglion Cell Responses
human_review_text:
This work is an important step in developing the tools for understanding the nonlinear response properties of visual neurons. The methods are sound and the results are meaningful. Reviewer 3 gave a much lower score than the other two reviewers because Rev 3 does not appreciate the improvement of prediction performance as an advance in itself. For understanding of the visual algorithms in the brain, however, prediction performance is the most critical success criterion. The paper provides convincing evidence that the approach is promising and likely to facilitate further advances towards achieving this long-term goal.
 
 I am confident enough to defend acceptance of this paper for a poster.

---

We have posted a new revision of the manuscript in which we changed the subset of cells for which we show results to better align with a previous study. The results remain unchanged. One of our example cells in Figure 3 was no longer in the criteria-passing subset so we are showing responses from a different OFF example cell. Additionally, we added a supplementary figure showing comparisons using a normalized log-likelihood metric, posted a link to a video of the stimulus, added “Responses” to the title, and made minor cosmetic changes to the figures.

---

This paper explores the ability of nonlinear recurrent neural networks to account for neural response properties that have otherwise eluded the ability of other models.  A multilayer rnn is trained to imitate the stimulus-response mapping measured from actual retinal ganglion cells in response to a sequence of natural images.  The rnn performs significantly better, especially in accounting for transient responses, than conventional LN/GLM models.

This work is an important step in understanding the nonlinear response properties of visual neurons.  Recent results have shown that the responses of even retinal ganglion cells in response to natural movies are difficult to explain in terms of standard receptive field models.  So this presents an important challenge to the field.  If we even had *a* model that works, it would be a starting point.  So this work should be seen in that light.  The challenge now of course is to tease apart what the rnn is doing.  Perhaps it could now be pruned and simplified to see what parts are critical to performance.  It would have been nice to see such an analysis.   Nevertheless this result is a good first start and I think important for people to know about.

I am a bit confused about what is being called a "movie."  My understanding is that it is essentially a sequence of unrelated images shown for 1 sec. each.  But then it is stated that the "frame rate" is 1/8.33 ms.  I think this must refer to the refresh rate of the monitor, right?   

I would guess that the deviations from the LN model are even stronger when you show actual dynamic natural scenes - i.e., real movies.  Here I would expect the rnn to have an even more profound effect, and potentially be much more informative.

---

This is a clearly written paper with a nice, if straightforward, result: RNNs can be good predictive models of neuron firing rates in the retina.

On the one hand, the primary scientific contribution seems to just be to confirm that this approach works. On this particular stimulus locked task the gains from using the RNN seemed relatively modest, and it hasn't yet taught us anything new about the biology.

On the other hand, this (along with the concurrent work of McIntosh et al.) is introducing neural network modeling to a field that isn't currently using it, and where it should prove very effective.

I think it would be very interesting to see the results of applying a framework like this one with LFP and other neurons as input and on a shorter discretization time scale.

I suspect followup work building on this proof of concept will be increasingly exciting.

Minor comments:
Sec 3.2:
I didn't understand the role of the 0.833 ms bins.
Use "epoch" throughout, rather than alternating between "epoch" and "pass through data".

Fig. 4 would be better with the x-axis on a log scale.

---

This paper fits models to spike trains of retinal ganglion cells that are driven by natural images. I think the title should thus include the word “activity” at the end for otherwise it is actually formally incorrect.

Anyhow, this paper proposes more specifically a recurrent network for this time series prediction and compares it to what seems to be the previous approach of a generalized linear model. Overall the stated paradigm is that when one can predict the spikes well then one can look into the model and learn how nature does it. 

In general the paper sounds plausible, though I am not convinced that I learned a lot. The results in figure 2 show that the RNN model can predict the spikes a bit better. So this is nice. But now what? You have shown that a more complicated model can produce better fits to the data, though there are of course still some variations to the real data. Your initial outline was that a better predictive model helps you to better understand the neural processing in the retina. So tell us what you learned. I am not a specialist of the retina, but I know that there are several layers and recurrencies in the retina, so I am not so surprised that the new model is better than the GLM. 

It seems that more complicated recurrent models such as LSTM do not improve the performance according to a statement in the paper. However, comparisons on this level are also difficult as a more complex models needs more data. Hence, I would actually expect that more layers and even a more detailed model of the retina could eventually improve the prediction even further. 
I was also a bit puzzled that all the neurons in the network share all the same parameters (weights). While the results show that these simplified models can capture a lot of the spike train characteristics, couldn’t a model with free parameters eventually outperform this one (with correspondingly more training data)?

structure_clarity.summary: The paper presents a study on modeling retinal ganglion cell responses using recurrent neural networks, comparing them with generalized linear models (GLMs). It details the methodology and data collection process, focusing on parasol cells in primate retina.
strengths: Clear introduction of the problem and existing methods
Detailed description of the experimental setup and model architecture
Comparison between GLMs and RNNs with a focus on predictive performance
weaknesses: Missing discussion section to interpret results and implications
Limited exploration of hybrid models in detail, only briefly mentioned
No mention of future work or potential extensions

methodology.summary: The draft introduces a multitask RNN approach to model retinal ganglion cell responses, comparing it with GLMs. It mentions using shared features across neurons and interleaving test data but lacks specific details on RNN architectures and hyperparameters.
strengths: Addresses the limitations of traditional GLM models by proposing a multitask RNN framework
Interleaves test data to address potential temporal drift issues
weaknesses: Lacks specification of RNN architectures (e.g., LSTM, GRU) and hyperparameters used in the experiments
No direct comparison against established GLM baselines for this task category is provided
methodology.needs_clarification: What specific RNN architectures were used (e.g., LSTM, GRU), and what were the hyperparameters for these models?

novelty.summary: The paper introduces multilayer recurrent neural networks for modeling primate retinal ganglion cell responses, outperforming GLMs in this context. However, the related work set is not rich enough to fully assess its novelty and citation coverage.
strengths: Introduces a novel approach using multitask RNNs for complex neuron response prediction.
Achieves good predictive performance with small training data.
weaknesses: The related work set lacks abstracts, making it difficult to fully evaluate the novelty of the proposed method.
Does not adequately cite or position itself against relevant literature on recurrent neural networks and their applications in neuroscience.

original_verdict.summary: The paper presents a comparison between generalized linear models (GLMs) and recurrent neural networks (RNNs), particularly multilayer RNNs, for modeling the spiking responses of parasol retinal ganglion cells to natural images. The authors use two separate experiments with multiple cells from each experiment, focusing on both ON and OFF cell types.
strengths: The paper compares GLMs against more complex models (RNNs) which can capture temporal dependencies better.
It uses a real-world dataset of natural images to test the models.
weaknesses: Specific RNN architectures and hyperparameters are not detailed, making it difficult to fully assess model performance.
The lack of comparison against established baselines for RNNs in this task category is noted. No specific RNN architecture or training details were provided.
The test data interleaving method is described but the exact split between train and test sets is unclear.
original_verdict.needs_clarification: What specific RNN architectures (e.g., LSTM, GRU) were used, what hyperparameters were set for these models, and how was the data split into training and testing sets?

debate_log.challenger_critique: The original review's critique about the lack of specific RNN architectures and hyperparameters is valid. However, the reviewer missed noting that the paper does mention using a multitask learning approach with shared features across neurons, which could be seen as an implicit comparison to other RNN architectures. Additionally, the interleaving method for test data described in the paper addresses the reviewer's concern about the exact split between train and test sets.

report.final_recommendation:
### Overall Summary

The paper proposes a multitask RNN approach for modeling retinal ganglion cell responses in primate retina, comparing it with traditional GLMs. The methodology is clear and well-documented, but lacks specific details on the RNN architectures and hyperparameters used. The comparison between models is compelling, showing good predictive performance with small training data. However, the related work set is limited, making it difficult to fully assess the novelty of the proposed method.

### Key Strengths

1. **Clear Introduction and Methodology**: The paper provides a clear introduction to the problem and existing methods.
2. **Detailed Experimental Setup**: A detailed description of the experimental setup and model architecture is provided.
3. **Good Predictive Performance**: Achieves good predictive performance with small training data.

### Key Weaknesses (Prioritized, Most Important First)

1. **Lack of Specific RNN Details**: The paper lacks specific details on the RNN architectures used (e.g., LSTM, GRU) and their hyperparameters.
2. **Missing Discussion Section**: No discussion section to interpret results and implications.
3. **Limited Exploration of Hybrid Models**: Only briefly mentioned without detailed exploration.

### Missing Sections / Information

- A discussion section to interpret the results and discuss their implications.
- More details on the RNN architectures used, including hyperparameters.
- Direct comparison against established GLM baselines for this task category.
- Future work or potential extensions.

### Significance Assessment

The contribution is promising but incremental. While the paper introduces a novel approach using multitask RNNs and demonstrates good predictive performance, the related work set is limited. The significance of the findings depends on whether the proposed method addresses critical limitations of GLMs in this context and how it can be extended or applied more broadly.

### Recommendation

The manuscript shows potential but requires significant revisions to address the identified weaknesses. Specifically, provide detailed information on RNN architectures and hyperparameters used, include a discussion section, and conduct a thorough comparison against established GLM baselines. If these issues are addressed adequately, the paper could be considered for submission. However, given the limited related work set, it may be beneficial to strengthen this aspect by incorporating more relevant literature.

**Final Recommendation**: **Major Revision Required Before Resubmission**. Address the missing details and ensure a comprehensive comparison with existing methods before resubmitting. Consider expanding the related work section to better contextualize the novelty of your approach.
